cards.title: Judge your subscription retention against your product's consumption model
cards.summary: Set realistic churn and LTV targets by classifying your product's natural usage frequency before benchmarking against other brands.
cards.use_when: Setting subscription targets or diagnosing churn and deciding whether your product genuinely supports a subscription offer.
steps: Classify your product by natural consumption frequency: daily-ritual goods (supplement powders, coffee, greens) support higher retention; occasion-only goods (CBD gummies, alcohol alternatives, seasonings) support lower retention and looser cadence.
Use that classification to set expected churn and LTV internally rather than comparing against brands in other niches — a daily powder and a seasonal seasoning have no comparable benchmark.
If your product is occasion-based, plan for higher churn and design cadences around usage rather than forcing a 30-day recurring model.
Note step zero is product quality — good product that people genuinely come back for is the prerequisite; no offer or onboarding fixes a product with no repeat use.
Use retention (paid-CAC repeat orders) as the primary profit lever, since re-acquiring buyers already paid for is cheaper than lowering CAC by a few percent.
caveats: Product-category retention differences are the presenter's observed pattern, not measured benchmarks — validate against your own cohort data.
The source's disclaimer to avoid 'just have a good product' advice applies here as a prerequisite, not a strategy.

cards.title: Subscription-first offer architecture: no discount on one-time, big discount on sub
cards.summary: Structure the PDP offer so subscription gets the discount and welcome kit while the one-time purchase stays full price, small and discreet.
cards.use_when: Designing or rebuilding the product page offer for a consumable product where you want first-order subscription take rate.
steps: Remove all discount and incentive from the one-time purchase — show it at full price, small and visually recessed so it's available but not attractive.
Put the entire offer (discount, welcome kit, guarantee, program access) on the subscription option only.
Build a welcome kit of physical add-ons with stated dollar value shown on the page, plus an optional zero-cost digital perk (course, wellness booklet) to inflate perceived value.
Apply the same offer in your email pop-up so the pop-up promotes the subscription deal, not a separate one-time discount.

Example structure the source cites: ~30% off a 90-day supply subscription plus a welcome kit (~$89 stated value), a guarantee, and access to a 90-day program — with one-time at full price and no bonus.
caveats: This is the source's recommended pattern based on subscribing brands it reviewed; test margin impact and one-time demand before removing all one-time discount.
Do not slash margins blindly — the presenter stresses the offer must be strong but profitability matters.

cards.title: Use a 3-option pricing display with two subscription choices
cards.summary: Show three purchase options on the PDP with two of them subscription-based to bias the default toward subscribing.
cards.use_when: Merchandising the buy-box on a subscription PDP to raise first-order take rate.
steps: Offer three options, e.g., 90-day subscription, 30-day subscription, one-time purchase — so the majority of visible choices are subscription.
Auto-select the subscription option on page load; humans default to what is pre-selected.
Make the one-time option the minority and visually smaller/less prominent.
Show the savings amount, perks, and free gifts inline on the subscription selections so the value gap is obvious.
Avoid the two-option layout where one-time is automatically selected — the source calls this an unoptimized PDP for take rate.
caveats: Source-specific tactic presented as a bias lever, not a proven universal rule; A/B test take-rate and downstream retention.
The presenter notes people also tend toward middle options — layout and ordering matter.

cards.title: Consumption-focused free gifts to reduce churn
cards.summary: Choose first-order gifts that physically help the customer use the product daily, not generic swag, because the top cancel reason is running out of use-habit.
cards.use_when: Selecting welcome-kit and in-subscription free gifts for a consumable product.
steps: Identify the friction that stops daily use (mixing, measuring, dosing) and pick low-cost supplementary items that remove it — e.g., a frother or quality spoon for a powder, a bottle for a drink.
Avoid generic branded items like stickers; the source explicitly warns against gifts that don't aid consumption.
For first-order gifts, focus entirely on consumption tools that build the daily habit.
For later in-subscription gifts, shift toward revenue expansion — sample packs of your other products — plus some branded items.
Never gift more of the same product in later shipments — extra same-product units cause customers to delay or cancel the next order.
Strategically place gifts at the high-churn months: the source names months 2, 4, and 6 as key churn points, but says gifting every order is optional.
caveats: Gifts only reduce churn if clearly communicated in billing reminders and order confirmations.
Month 2/4/6 churn points are the presenter's heuristic based on client cohorts, not a general benchmark.

cards.title: Match subscription cadence and quantity to real consumption
cards.summary: Set billing frequency and pack size so customers run out roughly when the next shipment arrives, avoiding 'too much product' cancellations.
cards.use_when: Configuring subscription cadence and quantity options on the PDP or in the portal.
steps: Estimate actual daily/weekly consumption per subscriber and set the default cadence to match.
Let customers choose quantity within a cadence — e.g., a beverage brand offering different can counts on a 30-day plan.
Avoid defaulting a daily-use product to a 30-day cadence that over-supplies, and avoid putting non-daily-use products on a 30-day cadence at all.
Watch 'too much product' cancellations as a signal that cadence or quantity defaults are wrong.
Example cited: a 48-can 30-day subscription for a single person is the kind of mismatch that drives cancellations.
caveats: Consumption rate is an estimate; use churn reasons and customer surveys to refine rather than assuming it.

cards.title: Build first-order subscription LTV case with cohort comparison
cards.summary: Compare 6-, 12-, and 24-month LTV of first-order-subscription vs non-subscription buyers to justify investing in take rate.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much offer value to spend to convert first orders into subscriptions, or building the business case internally.
steps: Segment customers by whether their first order included a subscription.
Pull 6-month LTV for each segment; the source's example brand showed ~$130 baseline vs ~$195 with first-order subscription (about +50%).
Extend to 12 and 24 months — the source reports roughly 2x by month 12 and 3x by month 24 in that example.
Use the multiple to size how much margin you can afford to give up in first-order subscription discount and welcome kit.
Treat the gap as the reason to optimize take rate, not CAC reduction, since these are already-acquired customers.
caveats: The 50%/2x/3x figures are one brand's example ('bare minimum standard numbers' per the source), not universal benchmarks — compute your own cohorts.
LTV differences reflect selection bias (subscription buyers may already be more committed), so attribute value carefully.

cards.title: Front-load onboarding education in days 1-7 before delivery
cards.summary: Send daily or near-daily education emails in the first week after purchase, timed to the pre-delivery window when cancellation risk is lowest.
cards.use_when: Designing the subscriber onboarding email/SMS sequence after first order.
steps: Send a founder thank-you and welcome email immediately at order placement.
Send daily (or at minimum every-other-day) education emails through days 1-7, before the product arrives — this is a low-cancellation window because customers haven't tried the product yet.
Include consumption instructions, ingredient education, and expected-timeline messaging.
Back off during days 7-14 (around delivery) — the source advises against daily emails then because each email reminds customers they could cancel.
Add a delivery-day consumption-tips email and optional one- or two-week check-ins.
Align SMS with email but send every other day rather than daily.
caveats: Cadence specifics (daily in days 1-7, back off days 7-14) are the presenter's pattern from client accounts, not a tested universal rule.
Every email is a cancellation prompt — limit volume while still communicating; the source does not recommend ghosting subscribers.

cards.title: Habit-stacking and long-term pacing messaging
cards.summary: Teach subscribers to attach product use to an existing daily habit and set a 90-120 day results timeline to prevent early cancellation.
cards.use_when: Writing onboarding and ongoing subscriber emails for a daily-use consumable.
steps: Survey customers on how they use the product, then find which usage context correlates with highest retention/LTV.
The source's example: a creatine brand found customers who mixed it into morning coffee had significantly higher retention than other groups because coffee is a fixed daily habit.
Immediately reorient onboarding messaging around that finding — repeatedly instruct customers to stack the product onto their existing habit.
Set explicit results expectations: tell customers to judge the product after 90-120 days, not immediately.
Avoid promising early results, which the source says causes cancellations at the promised point.
Reinforce consistently — 'people need to be reminded more than they need to be taught' — repeat tips across multiple emails.
caveats: Habit-stacking correlation may reflect other traits of those customers; validate with your own retention data before rewriting the whole sequence.

cards.title: Optimized billing reminder: lead with delay, bury cancel
cards.summary: Rebuild the pre-charge billing reminder with benefits and education, a prominent one-click delay/skip CTA, and the manage/cancel link at the very bottom.
cards.use_when: Editing the subscription billing reminder email (platform-native or in your ESP).
steps: Confirm sending a billing reminder is required in some states — the source says skipping it risks legal trouble and is poor brand practice; send it.
Move the reminder out of the subscription platform (e.g., Recharge, Skio) into your ESP for full design control; verify current platform capabilities.
Rewrite from scary transactional ('you'll be charged $X') to motivational, benefit-led copy that reiterates product perks and discount savings.
Add one-click 'delay order' / 'skip' action links at the top — the biggest cancel reason is too much product, so make the alternative easy.
Include upcoming free gifts and perks in the reminder; gifts only help if communicated.
Place the 'manage my subscription' / cancel link at the very bottom.
The source's client A/B test changed cancellations from 8.6% to 5.8% (about a 28-33% reduction) with this restructure.
caveats: The 8.6%→5.8% result is one brand's test; your baseline and outcome will differ.
Cancel-intent capture still needs a real cancel path elsewhere — this is a reminder email, not the cancellation flow.

cards.title: Customize billing reminders by refill number and product
cards.summary: Vary reminder copy by which refill the subscriber is on and which product they hold, especially highlighting upcoming gifts.
cards.use_when: Building segmented billing reminder templates for an active subscription base.
steps: Create separate reminder templates for first rebill, second, third, and later orders with different messaging for what the customer is experiencing.
If a gift ships on a specific order (e.g., order 3), rewrite that order's reminder to focus on the free gift — nobody cancels when something free is coming.
Segment by product subscribed so copy references their actual item.
Keep the same structural rules across all variants: delay CTA near the top, cancel link at the bottom.
Reaffirm perks each time — discount, gifts, pause/skip/cancel flexibility.
caveats: Requires platform/ESP segmentation capability and accurate order-number data; verify your tools support per-order dynamic content.

cards.title: Rebuild the order confirmation email off the platform default
cards.summary: Replace the clinical Shopify/native order confirmation with a branded, benefit-led, order-number-aware email to blunt the biggest churn spike.
cards.use_when: Optimizing transactional emails; especially where day-30 churn is high.
steps: Measure churn by day-since-subscription; the source's client showed the largest spike on day 30, when the first rebill confirmation lands.
Note the source says this confirmation can draw roughly double the cancellations of the billing reminder.

Identify if you're on Shopify Plus — the source says Plus stores must keep native order emails on; non-Plus stores can request Shopify support to disable them, then rebuild in the ESP (verify current Shopify policy).
Write confirmation copy that celebrates the order, restates product benefits, and includes testimonials where possible to remove the 'receipt' feel.
Customize by order number and by subscription vs one-time; if a gift booklet or product milestone applies, feature it.
Apply the same branded treatment to other transactional emails where practical.
caveats: Shopify Plus email-removal limitation is stated by the source and may change — verify with Shopify.
Source's day-30 spike is one audited 8-figure brand; measure your own churn curve.

cards.title: Exclude active subscribers from standard campaigns
cards.summary: Segment active subscribers out of generic promos and sales, and send them only 1-3 thoughtful campaigns monthly plus exclusive one-time add-on offers.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign sends to a list that includes active subscribers.
steps: Exclude active subscribers from standard sales and promo campaigns — otherwise they cancel to buy at the sale price.
Cap subscriber-targeted campaigns at roughly 1-3 per month; the source says every send is a prompt to reconsider subscribing.
Send a monthly founder newsletter to subscribers with community news, exclusive giveaways, or team spotlights to create exclusivity.
Offer subscribers a custom one-time add-on deal instead of the public sale — e.g., 30% off a protein powder added to their next subscription order.

The source's client example: over-sending to active subscribers produced enough cancels to make the subscription program net negative on campaigns; excluding them yielded about +24k/month net improvement and contributed to churn falling from ~19% to ~13-14%.
caveats: The ~19%→13-14% churn improvement was due to multiple changes, not campaigns alone (source acknowledged this).
Cap of 1-3 campaigns/month is the presenter's recommendation, not a tested threshold.

cards.title: Cancellation flow: founder splash screen then reason-based branching
cards.summary: Add a founder video splash on the cancel page and route each cancellation reason to a specific save action, targeting a 15%+ save rate.
cards.use_when: Building or tuning the in-portal subscription cancellation flow (e.g., Skio, Recharge).
steps: Add a splash screen on the cancel page with a personal founder video thanking the customer, reminding them of the mission, and pushing a delay/skip instead of full cancellation.
If you have a loyalty program, surface points-at-risk loss aversion before the reason survey.

Ask 'why are you cancelling?' and branch to a tailored action: too much product → delay/skip or change next order date; don't like taste → swap product; too expensive → discount offer; want a different product → swap product; taking a break → skip or change date.
Allow frequency edits where relevant.
Track save rate: source benchmarks 15%+ as good, ~20% strong, under 10% as a red flag needing work; one cited flow hit 14.6%.
caveats: Save-rate bands are the presenter's heuristics, not a formula — compare to your own baseline.
Discount offers should be segment-limited so they don't train customers to cancel for discounts.

cards.title: Immediate post-cancel flow plus delayed win-back at 30-60 days
cards.summary: Send one or two reason-specific reactivation emails right after cancellation, then a delayed win-back offer 30-60 days later with an escalated discount.
cards.use_when: Designing email flows for customers who just cancelled a subscription.
steps: Split the immediate post-cancel emails by the cancellation reason and address that specific pain point; include a reactivate option.
Follow with at most one 'last chance' email — the source says it's hard to win back immediately because the customer just went through the cancel flow.
Return cancelled customers to your regular campaign cadence, since they may organically re-buy.
If they still haven't returned, deploy a win-back flow 30-60 days after cancellation — the source reports more success here than immediately.
Test escalated offers in win-back: e.g., 30-50% off first subscription back, tapering to your standard ~15%.
Segment win-back by original cancellation reason and include a clear 'reactivate my subscription' CTA, plus founder faces and a heartfelt note.
caveats: Win-back timing (30-60 days) and discount levels (30-50%) are the presenter's recommendations from client work; test margin and response in your base.
Immediate post-cancel flows typically convert poorly — don't over-invest in optimizing them.
